## Test Coverage Signals — Coverage is a Smoke Alarm, Not a Goal

Line coverage tells you the test suite EXECUTED a line. It does not tell you the test suite would have FAILED if the line were wrong. A 100%-coverage suite can pass even when the code is broken.

### What coverage actually measures

- **Line coverage**: % of executable lines hit by tests. The default metric. The least informative.
- **Branch coverage**: % of conditional branches taken. More informative.
- **Mutation coverage** (PIT, Stryker, mutmut): the suite is run against intentionally-mutated versions of the code. % of mutants the suite catches. The most informative — directly measures the suite's ability to detect defects.

### The Mantu coverage policy

- **Minimum line coverage on new code: 80%** (per `mantu-sdlc-pipeline` Stage 1 gate)
- **Minimum line coverage on legacy code being modified: must not decrease**
- **Mutation coverage on critical business logic: > 75%** (run on a nightly or per-release cadence, not per-PR — it is slow)
- **0% coverage is rejected.** No exceptions, including "this is just a script." If it lives in source control and runs in production, it has tests.

### Anti-patterns coverage hides

- **Assertion-free tests**: the test executes the code (coverage goes up) but does not assert. These are noise. Mutation testing catches them; line coverage does not.
- **Coverage farming**: writing tests purely to hit lines. Tests that exist for the metric are worse than no tests — they create false confidence.
- **The 100% coverage trap**: pushing for 100% on trivial code (getters, setters, framework boilerplate) while critical paths are 40% covered. Cover the critical paths first.

## Fast Feedback — The Inner-Loop Speed Discipline

TDD only works if the test loop is fast. If running the suite takes 10 minutes, no engineer will run it on every save. If running the suite takes 5 seconds, every engineer runs it on every save.

### The Mantu inner-loop targets

| Test scope | Target time | What runs |
|---|---|---|
| Single test file (unit) | < 1 second | One file's tests |
| Module unit test suite | < 5 seconds | All unit tests in the module being worked on |
| Full unit test suite | < 30 seconds | Every unit test in the repo |
| Integration suite | < 5 minutes | Cross-module integration tests with real collaborators |
| End-to-end suite | < 30 minutes | Full system tests, browser automation, deployed-environment tests |
| Mutation testing | nightly | Slow by nature, not in the inner loop |

If the unit suite is over 30 seconds, the team has a problem worth a dedicated retro item. The friction compounds: slow suites get run less often; less-run suites accumulate failures; accumulated failures get suppressed ("known failing tests" lists); suppressed failures hide regressions; regressions ship.

### Speedup patterns

- **Parallelism**: run tests in parallel across CPU cores (jest --maxWorkers, vitest --pool=threads, pytest-xdist, go test -parallel)
- **Test isolation**: each test sets up its own state. Shared state is the enemy of parallelism.
- **Test database in-memory**: SQLite in-memory, testcontainers for full DB integration only
- **Watch mode**: jest --watch, vitest --watch, pytest-watch — re-run only affected tests on save
- **Sharding**: split the suite across CI machines for parallel execution in the build pipeline
- **Test pyramid discipline**: many fast unit tests, fewer slow integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. Inverting the pyramid (mostly E2E tests) is a guaranteed slow loop.

## Common Rationalisations

| Excuse | Reality |
|---|---|
| "We don't have time for TDD." | TDD is faster, not slower. The hour you save skipping the test costs three hours debugging the defect it would have caught. Measured across every engagement Mantu has run, TDD engagements ship at higher velocity AND lower defect rate. |
| "Tests are write-once, the code changes." | Behaviour-bound tests survive refactors. Implementation-bound tests don't. If your tests break every refactor, you are testing the wrong thing — fix the tests, don't abandon TDD. |
| "We'll add tests later." | "Later" never arrives. Even when it does, the tests are post-hoc and prove nothing about whether the implementation was correct when it was written. The window for valuable tests closes when the implementation is written. |
| "Our codebase is too complex for TDD." | The codebase is complex BECAUSE it was written without TDD. The complexity is the diagnostic. Adopt characterisation tests (Feathers) and TDD into the changes from this point forward. The codebase compounds in the right direction. |
| "The AI agent already wrote tests, we're good." | Audit trail required. Was the test written BEFORE the implementation diff? Did it RUN and report failure? Without the red-test artefact in the commit history, the AI rewrote the test to match its implementation. That is not TDD. |
| "100% line coverage means we're done." | Line coverage is a smoke alarm. Mutation coverage is the actual signal. A 100%-line-coverage suite can fail to catch trivial defects. Measure mutation coverage on critical paths. |
| "Mocks are slowing us down." | If mocks are slowing you down, you have over-mocked. Mock the boundary (HTTP, database, file system), not the in-process collaborators. Use fakes for stateful collaborators. |
| "Refactoring without tests is fine if you're careful." | "Careful" is not a strategy. The green suite is the safety net. No suite, no refactor — only "rewriting that you hope works." |
| "The test is asserting the implementation because the implementation IS the behaviour." | Almost certainly false. There is almost always a level of abstraction at which the behaviour is observable through the public interface. Find it. Test there. |
| "We can't TDD UI code." | You can. Test the component's behaviour through its props/state/events (React Testing Library, Vue Test Utils, Storybook interactions). Test the visual output via snapshot tests with explicit gates. End-to-end test the journey. |
| "TDD doesn't work for ML / data pipelines / infrastructure." | It does, with adapted tactics. ML: test the data shape, the loss-function direction, the deterministic transformations. Data pipelines: test the schema, the row-count contracts, the idempotence. Infrastructure: test the policy (OPA, Terratest), the smoke-deploy, the rollback. The pattern adapts to the domain. |
| "The legacy system has zero tests, we can't add tests now." | Characterisation tests (Feathers). They pin down CURRENT behaviour without you needing to know the original intent. Once you have them, you can refactor safely. This is exactly how Feathers' book unblocks the legacy-system case. |

## Red Flags — STOP and Restore the Discipline

- A PR merged to main with NO new or modified test file → STOP. Revert. Require red-green-refactor evidence.
- AI agent edited a production source file with no test edit in the same session → STOP. tdd-guard violation. Reject the change.
- Test file commit timestamp is AFTER the implementation commit timestamp → STOP. Tests were written post-hoc. Re-do the change with red-first.
- Test passes immediately when the test is added (no red phase) → STOP. The test is tautological or the implementation already exists. Find the actual missing behaviour or delete the false test.
- Refactor PR turned the suite red and was merged anyway → STOP. Revert. Re-do with green-throughout.
- Mock cascade > 4 layers deep in a single test → STOP. The module is over-coupled or the test is mocking the wrong boundary.
- Coverage is 95%+ but no mutation testing has ever run → STOP. The coverage number is uncalibrated. Run mutation testing once to baseline.
- Unit test suite takes > 60 seconds → STOP. Run a dedicated retro item on test suite performance.
- "Known failing tests" list exists in the repo → STOP. Each entry is a deferred regression. Fix or delete with documented reasoning.
- Test description reads `test_method_1`, `test_method_2` → STOP. Re-name to BDD-style behaviour descriptions before merge.
- Private method is being tested directly via reflection or visibility hacks → STOP. Test through the public interface or extract the private into its own publicly-tested module.
- Legacy code is being modified with no characterisation tests in place → STOP. Pin the current behaviour first.
- tdd-guard plugin is not installed on an AI-augmented engagement that has Edit/Write production authority → STOP. Install before the next AI commit.

**All of these mean: the TDD discipline is not running. Restore it before the next change ships.**

## Good vs Bad Example

### BAD

A Mantu engineering team is six weeks into a banking-data-platform engagement. The Senior System Engineer (Opus tier) is pair-coding with a Sonnet-tier AI agent. The team is under time pressure for a Stage 4 demo. The agent generates a customer-deduplication module in one turn — 240 lines of production code, with a 60-line test file generated in the same turn that asserts the implementation's exact behaviour. All tests pass on first run. The PR is merged.

Three weeks later, a regulator audit asks: "How do you know the deduplication logic correctly handles the GDPR 'right to erasure' case where a deleted customer's record should not match a new customer with the same email?" The team checks the test suite. The behaviour is not explicitly tested. The test was written by the agent to mirror what the implementation does, not what the behaviour SHOULD be. The agent's implementation does not handle the erasure-then-new-customer edge case. A customer record is leaked across what should have been a privacy boundary.

The incident escalates to the Mantu Tech Lead, the EM, the client CISO, and the regulator. The client withholds 8% of the engagement fee pending remediation. Mantu's win rate at sister banks drops 11% for the next bidding cycle.

Root cause in the post-incident review: no red-test artefact in commit history. The test was generated AFTER the implementation. The TDD discipline was nominally followed (test file existed) but operationally violated (test wrote itself from the implementation, never went red, never forced the behavioural-edge-case thinking that would have caught the GDPR scenario).

### GOOD

Same engagement signature. Same time pressure. Same agent pair.

Stage 1 of the SDLC pipeline has `mantu-tdd-discipline` loaded and the tdd-guard plugin installed in Codex with the project's custom instructions ("Banking-data-platform: all PII-touching modules require an explicit erasure-case test"). The custom instruction is a project-specific addition layered on the default TDD rule set.

The engineer prompts: "Build the customer deduplication module. Requirements from PRD section 4.2."

The agent (Opus, in plan mode) writes the test file FIRST:

```
describe("CustomerDeduplication", () => {
  it("matches two customers with the same email and same address");
  it("does NOT match a deleted customer's email to a new customer with the same email");
  it("matches case-insensitively on email but case-sensitively on address line 1");
  it("returns 'erasure-protected' for customers whose erasure flag is set");
  ...
});
```

The agent RUNS the tests. All fail. RED confirmed and captured in the session log.

The agent then writes the implementation. Re-runs the tests. All pass. GREEN confirmed. The commit is atomic with both files (test + implementation), and the commit message says: "Customer deduplication: 8 behaviours including GDPR erasure boundary. Red→Green confirmed."

The PR is reviewed in Stage 2 by the Code Review Agent (Sonnet). The reviewer cross-references the PRD section 4.2 against the test names. All acceptance criteria have a test. The Security Review Agent (Sonnet) runs `mantu-secure-coding-checklist` and notes the GDPR-erasure test passes — the audit trail is in place.

Stage 4 demo: the client asks about GDPR erasure. The engineer pulls up the test file and the commit history. The test was red on commit-1, green on commit-2. The behaviour is provably correct from the test perspective and the implementation perspective. The client is reassured. The audit passes on first review. The engagement renews at a 12% premium because of the visible discipline.

The cost difference: BAD cost ~€800K-1.2M of remediation plus the win-rate hit. GOOD compounds across the firm as a case study in `_Reference/SDLC Pipeline E2E Test.md`.

## Verification Checklist (for the engineer + reviewer)

At any point during the change, ask:

- [ ] Was a test written or modified BEFORE the implementation diff in this PR?
- [ ] Did the test actually FAIL on the first run? (Captured in commit message or session log.)
- [ ] Did the test then PASS after the implementation was written?
- [ ] Are the test names BDD-style — readable as behaviour descriptions, not as implementation steps?
- [ ] Is the test asserting OBSERVABLE OUTCOMES (return values, persisted state, emitted events) and NOT internal implementation details?
- [ ] Is the test using a REAL implementation for cheap deterministic collaborators and MOCK/STUB/FAKE only for expensive or non-deterministic boundaries?
- [ ] Is the mock-cascade depth ≤ 3 layers? (4+ is a smell.)
- [ ] Does the unit suite still run in < 30 seconds?
- [ ] Is line coverage on the new code ≥ 80%?
- [ ] Has mutation coverage been baselined on critical paths in this module within the last release cycle?
- [ ] If this is an AI-augmented change, is tdd-guard (or equivalent hook) ACTIVE on the engagement?
- [ ] If this is legacy code, were characterisation tests added BEFORE the change?
- [ ] Is the refactor phase complete and the suite still green?
- [ ] No "known failing tests" added to a suppression list?
- [ ] PR description references the test files or behaviour names (so the reviewer can locate the proof)?

**Fifteen checks. Any unchecked? The TDD discipline is not running. Restore it before merge.**

## Expert Frameworks This Skill Embodies

- **Kent Beck — `Test-Driven Development: By Example` (2002)** — the canonical text. Red-Green-Refactor cycle, the "fake it till you make it" tactic, triangulation, the test as design driver.
- **Robert C. Martin — `Clean Code` and `The Three Laws of TDD`** — (1) write no production code without a failing test, (2) write no more test than is sufficient to fail, (3) write no more production code than is sufficient to pass.
- **Dan North — `Introducing BDD` (2006)** — the reformulation of TDD around behaviour: given/when/then naming, the test as executable specification, behaviour-bound rather than method-bound tests.
- **Matt Pocock — deep modules and the public-interface testing pattern** — drawn from John Ousterhout's `A Philosophy of Software Design`. Tests bind to the narrow interface; the deep implementation can change without breaking tests.
- **Michael Feathers — `Working Effectively with Legacy Code`** — characterisation tests as the way into untestable systems. The seams concept. Adding tests where none exist as the prerequisite to any refactor.
- **John Ousterhout — `A Philosophy of Software Design`** — deep modules vs shallow modules. The information-hiding discipline that makes the public-interface testing pattern viable.
- **Martin Fowler — `Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code`** — the green-suite-as-safety-net pattern. Refactor is a verb that requires tests; without tests it is "rewriting and hoping."
- **Steve Freeman & Nat Pryce — `Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests`** — the outside-in TDD pattern, the role of mocks in driving design, the London-school TDD.
- **Stryker / PIT / mutmut — mutation testing tooling** — the calibration mechanism for whether the test suite actually catches defects. Line coverage as smoke alarm; mutation coverage as the real signal.
- **nizos/tdd-guard — the AI-TDD enforcement plugin** — the operational expression of TDD for AI-augmented engineering. Hook-based interception of Edit/Write/MultiEdit. Validates that a red test precedes any production code change. The pattern, not just the tool, is what Mantu adopts.

This skill is adapted from `nizos/tdd-guard` (the AI-TDD enforcement Codex plugin) combined with the foundational TDD literature (Beck, Martin, Fowler, Feathers, North), the deep-module testing pattern (Pocock, Ousterhout), and the Mantu-specific operational context (regulated clients, AI-augmented teams, multi-team coordination). The tdd-guard contribution is the AI-specific enforcement layer; the rest is the doctrine that makes the enforcement meaningful.

## Final Rule

```
TDD discipline run on every change → Mantu engineering work
TDD discipline skipped → a codebase that happens to have some tests
```

The difference between those two is the defect rate, the regulator-audit pass rate, the renewal premium, and whether AI agents are an accelerant or a liability on the engagement.

The test is the design. The test is the spec. The test is the audit trail. The test is what makes the difference between engineering and improvisation.
